strengths: Significance/originality: The paper targets an important emerging systems problem—serving tool-augmented LLMs whose execution is interrupted by external calls. Incorporating call duration, returned-token length, and KV-cache handling into scheduling is a useful extension beyond ordinary length-aware LLM schedulers.

Methodology: The combination of prediction-based admission ordering, post-call priority correction, and memory-aware token batching is coherent at a high level and is implemented in vLLM rather than evaluated only in simulation.

Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover two workloads, three GPU configurations, two model sizes, Poisson and bursty Gamma arrivals, fixed-duration and fixed-request settings, tail latency, SLO attainment, and component ablations.
Presentation: The system motivation and high-level architecture are generally understandable, and the paper clearly connects head-of-line blocking to goodput under latency SLOs.
weaknesses: Soundness: The stated anti-starvation mechanism appears to have the wrong sign. Requests with lower estimated cost are prioritized, yet Eq. 26 and Algorithm 1 add positive alpha times waiting time to the value being sorted. Under ascending cost order, waiting therefore lowers rather than raises priority. The paper neither specifies a negative alpha nor explains an opposite sort direction, so its fairness claim is unsupported and the mechanism may aggravate starvation.

Soundness: Important parts of the scheduler are underspecified or inconsistent. Stage I is said to use predicted API return length, but the prediction module predicts only output length and call duration, and Eqs. 13–15 contain no return-length estimate. It is also unclear what an output prediction means across multiple tool-call rounds. The cost formulas are heuristic and receive no validation against measured execution or memory cost.

Soundness/evidence: The comparison isolates the proposed scheduler only against FCFS-based vLLM and InferCept. It omits the length-aware/SJF, learned-ranking, and preemptive schedulers discussed in the related-work section. Since reordering overloaded FCFS queues is the principal source of the very large gains, the experiments do not establish that the proposed two-stage cost model is better than simpler scheduling alternatives such as predicted remaining processing time or aging-aware SJF.

Evidence: Many headline multiplicative gains occur where baseline goodput has nearly collapsed under a strict one-second TTFT SLO. Absolute AugServe goodput can remain far below offered load—for example, Table 3 reports 0.51 req/s at 4 req/s on Merge—yet backlog growth, completed-request throughput, timeout/drop policy, and latency of unfinished requests are not reported. This makes the claimed stability under sustained overload difficult to interpret.

Evaluation rigor: Results lack repeated trials, variance/error bars, confidence intervals, and seed information. There is no sensitivity study for alpha, beta_low, beta_high, gamma, or the offline-profiled target_max, nor an oracle-prediction comparison or controlled degradation study despite only 65% output-length accuracy on Merge. Thus robustness to tuning and prediction error is not convincingly demonstrated.

External validity: Evaluation is restricted to GPT-J-6B and OPT-13B and apparently replays two datasets. The manuscript does not adequately explain trace construction, API timing/return simulation, numbers of tool calls per request, sampling, or whether external tools are executed live. Modern agentic models, multi-round tool workflows, and changing API latency distributions are not evaluated.

Reproducibility: No code or artifact availability is stated. Crucial details are missing, including vLLM/InferCept versions and modifications, predictor architecture despite calling BERT-base 'only millions' of parameters, bucket boundaries, training hyperparameters and overhead, exact workload preprocessing, baseline tuning, hardware/software configuration, and all scheduler/batching parameter values. The reported API-duration 'mean squared error' is expressed in seconds rather than squared seconds and is ambiguously mapped to the datasets.

Presentation: Several definitions and equations are malformed or ambiguous, including Eq. 7's policy selection, inconsistent swap-rate notation, and whether queue sorting is ascending. Numerous grammatical issues and very small multi-panel plots further impede verification of exact results.

Limitations/ethics: The paper has no substantive limitations discussion. Cost-based prioritization can systematically delay long prompts or particular tool/API classes, and the proposed fairness safeguard is both unvalidated and apparently sign-inverted. Per-group waiting-time distributions, worst-case delay bounds, admission control, and operational risks from predicted API behavior are not addressed. No other material research-ethics issue is evident, but these service-fairness concerns warrant explicit treatment.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important systems problem—meeting latency SLOs for tool-augmented LLM serving, where external calls and heterogeneous sequence lengths complicate scheduling and KV-cache management.

Originality: Combining prediction-based initial scheduling, post-call priority correction, and memory-aware token-budget adjustment is a coherent design tailored to augmented inference. Incorporating API-return behavior and context-handling policies goes beyond ordinary output-length scheduling.

Evaluation breadth: The authors implement the system on vLLM and test two models, two workloads, three GPU configurations, Poisson and bursty arrivals, and both fixed-time and fixed-request settings. They report goodput, SLO attainment, mean and P95 latency, TPOT, and a component ablation.

Presentation: The motivation and high-level architecture are generally understandable. The empirical examples clearly illustrate that FCFS scheduling and a fixed token limit can perform poorly under heterogeneous workloads.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed anti-starvation mechanism appears mathematically reversed. The paper states that smaller predicted costs receive priority, but Equation 26 and Algorithm 1 add a positive multiple of waiting time to that cost. Ascending sorting would therefore lower the priority of requests the longer they wait, exacerbating rather than preventing starvation. No fairness or maximum-wait results resolve this inconsistency.

Soundness: The fixed-duration evaluation is vulnerable to censoring and selection bias. At several offered loads, goodput remains far below the arrival rate, so queues are apparently unstable. A shortest-job-oriented scheduler can report excellent TTFT and SLO attainment for selected short requests while indefinitely postponing expensive requests. The paper does not report backlog growth, unfinished-request counts, per-length-class attainment, maximum waiting time, or whether queues are drained after the 30-minute window.

Soundness and originality: The principal comparison is only against FCFS-based vLLM and InferCept. The related-work section itself identifies several prediction-based or shortest-job-first LLM schedulers, yet none is adapted or evaluated. Consequently, the very large gains mainly establish that informed reordering beats FCFS under overload, not that the proposed cost model or two-stage design advances the strongest applicable scheduling methods. The ablation also lacks simple predicted-length SJF, oracle-length scheduling, and one-stage scheduling controls.

Methodological clarity: Central experimental details are absent, including whether API calls and their durations are replayed, simulated, or executed live; workload length and call distributions; decoding parameters; baseline versions and tuning; queue-draining rules; repetitions, variance, and confidence intervals. This makes the reported 3.3–33.1x gains difficult to validate.

Reproducibility: No code or artifact availability statement is provided. Important parameters and procedures—including alpha, beta_low, beta_high, target_max, bucket boundaries, predictor architecture details, optimizer and training settings, profiling procedure, and dataset preprocessing—are unspecified. The random train/test splits may also leak API or template identity, while predictor robustness under workload shift is not evaluated.

Technical specification: Stage I is said to use predicted API return length, but Section 4.2 describes prediction only for output length and call duration, and the Stage-I cost equations do not clearly include predicted return length. Equation 7 is malformed, several cost models assume a constant iteration time despite changing batches, and the lower bound on the dynamic token budget is not shown to remain safe when actual available memory is smaller.

Presentation: Several plots are too small to read reliably, captions incorrectly say 'lower right is better,' and the prose contains frequent grammatical errors. More importantly, strong causal statements about stability and user experience are made without the backlog and fairness evidence needed to support them.

Limitations and ethics: There is no meaningful limitations discussion. Length-based prioritization can systematically disadvantage complex requests, particular tools, or users associated with longer contexts; this concern is especially material because the stated starvation safeguard appears incorrect. The paper does not examine per-group service quality, multi-tenant fairness, adversarial predictions, or privacy implications of training a request-content predictor. No otherwise severe research-ethics issue is apparent, but these deployment concerns should be acknowledged and evaluated.

strengths: The paper identifies an important systems problem: tool calls introduce pauses, uncertain return lengths, and context-management costs that conventional LLM serving schedulers do not model well. Improving SLO attainment for these workloads would be practically significant.

AugServe combines a tool-aware, two-stage scheduler with adaptive token batching in a coherent design. Revising priorities after observing actual API returns is a sensible way to limit errors from admission-time predictions, and the memory-based batching rule complements the scheduler.

The evaluation covers two workloads, three GPU configurations, two model families, Poisson and bursty arrivals, fixed-time and fixed-request experiments, average and tail latency, goodput, and SLO attainment. The reported improvements are large and generally consistent across these settings.

The manuscript is well organized and motivates its design with useful measurements. The cost model, scheduling phases, dynamic batching mechanism, and system integration are described at a reasonably understandable conceptual level.
No major research-ethics concern is apparent from the reported use of public workloads and local serving experiments.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not compare against a competitive length-aware or learned scheduling method, despite citing several such systems. The central scheduling contribution is primarily compared with FCFS-based vLLM and InferCept, so the very large gains do not establish that AugServe outperforms modern scheduling alternatives. A tuned shortest-job/estimated-size baseline and a dynamic-batching baseline are essential.

The ablation is too coarse to support the claimed benefits of the individual design choices. It does not separately evaluate Stage I versus Stage II, predicted versus oracle request features, the anti-starvation mechanism, prediction-error sensitivity, or alternative scheduling cost functions. Consequently, it remains unclear which parts are necessary and how robust the scheduler is to its relatively weak Merge prediction accuracy of 65%.

There is an apparent correctness ambiguity in the anti-starvation rule. Lower estimated cost is described as receiving higher priority, yet Equation 26 and Algorithm 1 add a positive multiple of waiting time to that cost. Under ascending-cost sorting, this penalizes long-waiting requests rather than promoting them. The sorting direction and sign must be clarified, and fairness/starvation should be measured rather than asserted.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper provides no code or artifact information and omits crucial settings such as alpha, beta_low, beta_high, target_max, prediction buckets and training hyperparameters, software versions, decoding parameters, API-duration construction, trace preprocessing, and baseline tuning. Results also lack repeated trials, variability, or confidence intervals.

Workload realism is insufficiently documented. It is unclear whether external tools are actually executed, whether delays and returned text are replayed or synthesized, how multi-round interactions are represented, and whether train/test splitting prevents overlap among related prompts or API types. Experiments use only 6B and 13B models and do not include a production trace or contemporary larger-model deployment.

Several reported robustness results require further explanation. For example, Merge goodput at 2 req/s rises from 0.87 at CV=1 to 1.15 at CV=1.5 before falling, contradicting the accompanying statement that efficiency declines as burstiness increases. Some headline values also differ slightly between the abstract and body, and the extreme baseline degradation warrants validation with error bars and configuration details.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations discussion. Its dependence on workload-specific predictors and offline profiling, possible degradation under distribution shift, scheduler overhead at larger concurrency, quality-of-service trade-offs for long requests, and applicability to multi-GPU or larger-model serving are not addressed. Because the method explicitly reorders users, fairness is also a material systems concern.

Overall, the idea is promising and the empirical results are encouraging, but the missing competitive baselines, unresolved scheduling-rule ambiguity, and insufficient experimental specification prevent the central performance claims from being considered fully supported or reproducible.

strengths: Soundness: The paper identifies a credible systems bottleneck in augmented-LLM serving and proposes a coherent design combining state-aware scheduling, runtime feedback, context-policy awareness, and a memory-sensitive token budget. The ablation in Table 2 supports the claim that scheduling is the main contributor and that dynamic budgeting provides an additional benefit.

Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover two datasets, four model configurations from GPT-J-6B to Llama-3-70B, several GPU platforms, multiple arrival rates, bursty and mixed workloads, prediction-error injection, tail latency, memory occupancy, and scheduling overhead. AugServe generally improves goodput and latency consistently, including against the stronger SSJF and reimplemented MARS baselines.

Significance: Efficient serving during external tool calls is an increasingly relevant problem. The reported improvements are large, and the approach could be practically useful if the results and implementation can be reproduced.

Originality: Modeling requests as evolving service segments and refining a space-time scheduling cost after tool returns provides a useful augmented-inference-specific extension to conventional length- or memory-based SJF scheduling.

Presentation: The paper is organized clearly, with a helpful lifecycle model, system overview, pseudocode, notation table, and readable experimental plots. The appendix appropriately limits the stated approximation guarantee to a simplified per-iteration problem.
Ethics: This is a low-risk infrastructure contribution, and no material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The optimization objective in Equations 2–4 does not directly encode either stated SLO or goodput. The paper therefore lacks a formal or empirical bridge showing that maximizing the proposed value-density surrogate maximizes SLO-constrained throughput, especially across future segments and tool-return events.

The theoretical result does not describe the implemented algorithm. Appendix E requires scanning past items that do not fit and returning the better of greedy packing and the best singleton. Algorithm 1 instead breaks at the first non-fitting request and contains no best-singleton comparison. Consequently, the claimed 1/2 guarantee does not apply to the presented AugServe procedure.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript provides no code or artifact information and omits important implementation details, including software versions, predictor training procedure and data splits, precise input metadata, profiling of the space-time cost terms, workload sizes/seeds, external-call replay methodology, token-budget bounds, reference budgets, and most baseline configurations.

The predictor is trained and evaluated on ToolBench and INFERCEPT, but the train/test separation is not specified. This creates a material risk of leakage and leaves uncertain how prediction quality and scheduling gains transfer to unseen requests, APIs, call-duration distributions, or workload shifts. Injecting symmetric multiplicative noise into existing predictions does not resolve this concern.

The empirical evidence lacks repeated trials, confidence intervals, or error bars. Given queueing systems' sensitivity to arrival traces and the use of 30-minute runs, it is unclear whether smaller differences are statistically stable.

The headline results are internally inconsistent: the abstract and introduction report geometric-mean goodput gains of 6.5× and 4.7× over vLLM and INFERCEPT, whereas Section 6.1 reports 7.5× and 5.7×. The exact aggregation set is not disclosed, making the central quantitative claim difficult to verify.

Baseline fairness remains insufficiently documented. MARS is reimplemented using the authors' prediction interface, but fidelity to the original system is not established; other relevant scheduling/preemption systems are discussed but not evaluated. It is also unclear whether every baseline receives equally optimized batch budgets and context-handling facilities.

The evaluation does not report serving quality or fairness across request classes. A density scheduler can systematically delay large or tool-heavy requests; the aging term is intended to prevent starvation, but only limited beta sensitivity is shown, with P99 TTFT still reaching roughly 99–157 seconds at the default setting.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: context-policy selection is inherited from INFERCEPT, value-density greedy scheduling is classical, and dynamic token budgeting is conceptually straightforward. The contribution lies mainly in their augmented-serving integration and state-dependent cost construction.

Limitations are not treated adequately. There is no substantive limitations section discussing dependence on predictable call behavior, centralized single-engine assumptions, external-service failures, multi-tenancy, fairness, or profiling portability. The impact statement is generic rather than an analysis of relevant operational risks such as resource allocation among tenants.

strengths: The paper targets an important systems problem: external calls create heterogeneous pause, cache-residency, and resumption behavior that conventional FCFS LLM serving does not model. Combining state-aware scheduling with adaptive batch capacity is a sensible direction with practical significance.

The evaluation covers two datasets, several model and GPU configurations, Poisson and bursty arrivals, mixed tool/non-tool traffic, and a 70B multi-GPU setting. The reported improvements over FCFS-based vLLM and INFERCEPT are large, and comparisons with SSJF and MARS provide some evidence beyond weak FCFS baselines.

The ablation separates state-aware scheduling from dynamic token budgeting, and the appendices examine prediction perturbations, beta sensitivity, scheduling overhead, tail latency, SLO attainment, and cache occupancy. The presentation is generally organized, and the request-lifecycle model is easy to follow.

The work has moderate originality: cache-policy selection builds substantially on INFERCEPT and density-based scheduling is classical, but applying cross-round runtime feedback and space-time costs to tool-augmented inference is a useful synthesis.
weaknesses: The optimization formulation does not justify the implemented heuristic. Equation 3 constrains instantaneous memory m_i(t), whereas the priority in Equation 4 divides value by an integrated space-time cost C_i,k. Thus this is not the value-to-weight greedy rule for the stated knapsack problem. More seriously, Algorithm 1 stops at the first item that does not fit and never evaluates the best feasible singleton, while Appendix E proves a 1/2 approximation only for an algorithm that scans past non-fitting items and returns the better of greedy packing and the best singleton. The advertised theoretical result therefore does not apply to the presented algorithm.

Central cost and budget calculations are underspecified and potentially unsound. The paper does not explain how future prefill, decode, call, recomputation, and swap space-time costs are estimated in practice. Equation 11 treats free plus reclaimable KV memory divided by a per-token footprint as an executable token budget, without accounting clearly for activation/workspace memory, reclamation timing, or preemption cost. The clipping constants, reference budget, profiling procedure, and most implementation parameters are not reported.

The predictor evaluation is inadequate for its central scheduling role. There are no training/test split sizes, feature definitions, training hyperparameters, leakage controls, or cross-workload generalization results. Reporting an external-call-duration “mean squared error” in seconds is dimensionally incorrect. The synthetic robustness test merely multiplies predictions by symmetric noise and does not reproduce realistic heavy-tailed API latency, categorical policy mistakes, or distribution shift. Calling a 10–20 second TTFT increase “mild” is also inconsistent with the paper's 1-second TTFT SLO.

The empirical evidence lacks essential statistical and workload details: request counts after filtering, tool-call counts per request, concurrency limits, call replay/emulation methodology, run-to-run variation, repetitions, confidence intervals, and failure handling are absent. Goodput ratios are especially unstable when baseline goodput is described as near zero, yet the geometric-mean aggregation and treatment of zero values are not specified. Consequently, the very large 6.5x/4.7x headline claims cannot be independently assessed.

Baseline fairness remains unclear. vLLM, INFERCEPT, SSJF, and MARS differ in cache handling as well as scheduling, and MARS is reimplemented without enough validation or tuning information. The paper does not provide controlled comparisons in which only the scheduling priority changes under identical cache-policy and batch-budget machinery. This makes it difficult to attribute gains specifically to the claimed state-aware cost model.

The evaluation exposes unresolved fairness and tail-latency concerns. Table 5 reports P99 TTFT around 99–157 seconds for the selected beta despite a 1-second SLO, suggesting severe starvation or very poor service for a subset of requests. There is no completion-rate, slowdown-by-request-size, starvation-bound, or per-class fairness analysis, so high goodput may be achieved partly by favoring inexpensive requests while sacrificing long ones.

Reproducibility is insufficient for acceptance: no code or artifact is identified, and the manuscript omits enough dataset preprocessing, predictor, profiling, system-configuration, and baseline details that reproducing the system and headline results would be difficult. The impact statement is boilerplate; although no major ethical hazard is apparent, it misses the relevant risk that efficiency-oriented scheduling may systematically disadvantage long or tool-heavy requests. Overall, the promising idea and broad-looking experiments do not overcome the formulation/algorithm inconsistency and insufficiently supported central empirical claims.

strengths: Soundness: The central systems idea is technically plausible and well motivated: AugServe models external-call requests across execution segments, refines priorities using realized return lengths and context-handling outcomes, and adjusts the token budget using both free and reclaimable KV-cache memory.

Evaluation: The paper reports broad experiments spanning two datasets, four model configurations from GPT-J-6B to Llama-3-70B-Instruct, several GPU platforms, Poisson and bursty arrivals, mixed tool/non-tool workloads, tail latency, SLO attainment, memory occupancy, prediction noise, and scheduling overhead.

Empirical results are consistently favorable. The main evaluation reports 7.5x/5.7x geometric-mean goodput improvements over vLLM/INFERCEPT, while the ablation improves goodput from 0.15 to 0.93 req/s with state-aware scheduling and to 1.07 req/s with the full system, indicating that the proposed scheduler is the main contributor and the adaptive budget provides an additional benefit.

Significance and originality: Efficient serving of tool-augmented LLMs is an increasingly important problem. Jointly accounting for multi-stage execution state, context-resumption cost, runtime feedback, and reclaimable memory is a useful advance over FCFS and ordinary length-based SJF scheduling.

Presentation: The request-lifecycle model, architecture, equations, pseudocode, and ablations make the design relatively easy to follow. The appendix appropriately qualifies the limited scope of its approximation result rather than overstating it.

Ethics and limitations: The work primarily changes serving efficiency and presents no evident material ethical risk. It honestly notes that the approximation result does not cover the full online scheduling problem.
weaknesses: Soundness: The theoretical result does not describe Algorithm 1 as written. The theorem returns the better of density-greedy packing and the best singleton and allows scanning past an item that does not fit, whereas Algorithm 1 has no best-singleton comparison and stops at the first non-fitting request. Moreover, scheduling is ranked by space-time cost while packing is constrained by active tokens, so the stated knapsack approximation does not directly characterize the implemented scheduler.

The cost model is underspecified operationally. Equations 5-10 define space-time costs through quantities such as residency duration, decode cost, return-token cost, and recomputation/swap cost, but the paper does not explain sufficiently how all these quantities are estimated online, calibrated across hardware, or converted into comparable priority values.

Baseline fairness needs stronger documentation. MARS is reimplemented under the authors' prediction interface, but implementation fidelity is not validated; versions, tuning procedures, and token-budget choices for vLLM, INFERCEPT, SSJF, and MARS are not reported in enough detail to rule out configuration effects. Comparisons with other modern goodput/deadline-aware schedulers are also limited.

The largest gains occur when FCFS baselines are severely overloaded—for example, average TTFT reaches roughly 300 seconds despite a 1-second TTFT SLO and baseline goodput approaches zero. Results near each system's sustainable capacity, latency-throughput frontiers, confidence intervals, and repeated-run variability would make the geometric-mean improvement claims substantially more convincing.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate for an Accept-level systems paper. There is no stated code/artifact release, and important details are missing: predictor training-set sizes and splits, features and optimization settings, replay of external-call durations, random seeds and trial counts, precision and parallelism settings, software versions, and values or tuning rules for beta_low, beta_high, and T_max.

The headline numbers are not fully reconciled: the abstract reports 6.5x and 4.7x goodput over vLLM and INFERCEPT, whereas Section 6.1 reports 7.5x and 5.7x. The aggregation sets producing these different geometric means should be stated explicitly.

The robustness experiment injects symmetric multiplicative noise independently, which may not resemble systematic or heavy-tailed prediction errors encountered under workload shift. Notably, the paper calls an additional 10-20 seconds of TTFT 'mild' even though its stated TTFT SLO is 1 second.

The impact statement is boilerplate and the limitations discussion omits practical concerns such as starvation/fairness across request classes, predictor distribution shift, behavior under failed or extremely long tool calls, and the added energy or CPU-memory costs of swapping and prediction.
